title: Law and mercy
hookLine: the law is meant to bring ease: Allah wants ease for you (2:185)

cards: A Bedouin man is urinating on the floor of the mosque in Medina, and the companions are already on their feet, shouting at him. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells them to leave him alone.
Let him finish, then pour a bucket of water over the spot. And, in the report in Sahih al-Bukhari, he tells them they were sent to make things easy, not hard.
Afterward he speaks gently to the man about what a mosque is for. A floor can be washed. A person driven away is harder to bring back.

teach.h: EASE, IN THE MIDDLE OF A RULE.
teach.b: The key line sits in the fasting verses of surah two.
Right after allowing the sick and the traveler to make up their fast on other days, the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you."
Not in a poem about mercy, but in the middle of a rule. The ease is part of the law, not an exception to it. The jurists built on this.
A traveler may shorten the prayers. Someone without water, or too ill to use it, may wipe with clean earth instead of washing, a practice called tayammum.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, a man with an illness asks how to pray, and the Prophet tells him: stand, and if you can't, sit, and if you can't, lie on your side. Each step down is still prayer.
These easings are called rukhsah, a permission, and a report in Musnad Ahmad says God loves His permissions to be taken.

teach.h: HE CHOSE THE EASIER, IF NOT A SIN.
teach.b: Aisha reports, also in Bukhari, that whenever the Prophet was given a choice between two matters he chose the easier, as long as it was not a sin.
That last clause matters: ease isn't anything goes, and the law still has edges.
Inside them, the default is mercy, and scholars made it a maxim: hardship brings ease. So a teacher who makes the law heavier than it is can be corrected from inside the tradition itself.

how: Muslims who are traveling, ill or unable to keep a rule in full use the permissions the law gives, such as shortening prayers, making up fasts later, praying seated, or wiping with clean earth when water can't be used.

o: a judge's power to cancel any rule he finds too hard
ease built into the law, with permissions for the weak
forgiveness offered after a rule is broken, not before

games.q: law and mercy — tap the pairs.
p: a permission that eases a rule
he chose the easier, if not a sin

s: in Islamic law, taking an easing permission is a weaker kind of faith
a report in Musnad Ahmad says God loves His permissions to be taken.
the verse about ease sits in the middle of the rules on fasting
it follows the permission for the sick and traveler to fast on other days.
choosing the easier path means anything goes
Aisha's report adds: as long as it was not a sin.

games.q: you're a companion in the mosque. a Bedouin starts urinating in the corner, and everyone jumps up shouting. what does the Prophet tell you to do?
o: leave him alone, then pour water over the spot.
games.why: he tells them to let the man finish and pour a bucket of water over it: you were sent to make things easy, not hard.

practice: Find one place where you've made something harder than it needs to be: a rule you keep for yourself, a standard you hold a friend to, a habit at work that only adds weight.
Ask whether the hard way is required or just habit, and if an easier way crosses no line, picture choosing it and notice your shoulders. If you pray, you can remember the verse about ease.

wordCard.voice: Law and mercy. In Islam, the law itself carries ease: permissions for the sick, the traveler and the weak, and a preference for the easier path where no sin is involved. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a permission; an easing the law gives in hardship.

carryVoice: Your line: ease, not hardship. The bucket of water comes before the shouting. Until tomorrow.
